body.p: Firstly, I would like to express my gratitude to our esteemed readers, contributors, and all individuals who actively participate in the review process of Arthroplasty Today.

That said, the number of submissions continues to grow annually, as does the number of citations and impact factor. While these metrics are positive indicators of the journal’s success, they also present challenges in managing the workload and ensuring the high quality of reviews for each submission. I, therefore, urge you to “pay it forward” by getting involved. If you are an author, researcher, or just a reader of the journal, any contribution to the review process would be welcome. In just looking at the numbers, we would have an excess of reviewers if all authors who submitted an article performed 2-3 reviews annually.

To enhance our reviewer recruitment efforts, we have initiated a mentorship program for fifth-year residents transitioning into arthroplasty. These residents will be matched with an editorial board member, receiving comprehensive training in conducting accurate and thorough reviews. If you have any residents interested in getting involved, please reach out (see below). We strongly encourage fellowship directors to have their fellows become reviewers. This serves as an excellent stepping stone to involvement in the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons (AAHKS) leadership. For many, this has led to roles on the editorial board, an associate editor position, and AAHKS committees.

Additionally, we have established an elite reviewer program for high-level reviewers willing to take on one article per month and deliver high-quality reviews within 2 weeks. This program offers further exposure to leadership and opportunities for future advancement. Reviewers will also be listed on the journal website and receive a discounted publication rate. Furthermore, the top 2 reviewers annually are invited to join the editorial board at Arthroplasty Today. While these may not be the most enticing offers to solicit for reviewers, they represent our current capabilities and may evolve into a scored Continuing Medical Education (CME) program in the future. AAHKS is an exceptional organization, and I encourage all members to take pride in their membership. By contributing to the journal’s continued success, we can achieve greater heights. Please consider getting involved!

Volume 38 is packed with fantastic original research articles, case reports and systematic reviews. Some of the articles to highlight include: An important project assessing the risks for readmission after same-day discharge total hip arthroplasty. Not to spoil the article, but the authors noted that increasing patient age and general anesthesia may impact these outcomes, read the full article to get the scoop. One of the technology-related articles covers the comparable accuracy of a mixed-reality system with that of robotics in total knee arthroplasty. Furthermore, there is an excellent article looking at full motion arc, laxity-based planning for total knee arthroplasty cases. This high-level planning may indeed be the next milestone for enabling technology. In keeping with the technology and planning theme, you should definitely read the article on complication risks associated with deviation from preoperative planning with an artificial intelligence implant predicting program. The last original research highlight involves the Michigan Arthroplasty Registry, which has become a powerful tool to assess large amounts of information from a high-quality database. The authors were able to leverage this information to create a novel preoperative calculator to predict 90-day prosthetic joint infection risk. Lastly, there is a nicely done case report describing the squeaky hip and if this extraneous noise is truly important.

All in all, this is another well-rounded volume for Arthroplasty Today. I do hope you enjoy reading these articles and get a better understanding of the growing amount of work that is required to keep the journal moving forward. In the future, we will have editorials covering current advocacy issues, physician well-being, and tips on proper ergonomics to prevent injury for arthroplasty surgeons. For all readers, and particularly authors, I urge you to consider paying it forward by becoming involved in the review process, editorial board, or other roles that we have available with Arthroplasty Today. As a product of our own success, it is imperative to have the help of AAHKS members to keep this train rolling while providing prompt reviews of the outstanding manuscripts we receive. I urge you all to participate, and if you have any questions on getting involved, you can reach me directly at brettlevinemd@gmail.com. I am always open to suggestions and encourage you to help us all at Arthroplasty Today in providing the highest quality product for our members and readers. Again, please help in paying it forward to our organization and its representative journal.
